locator.heading: Calamint, Or Mountain-Mint

source_text:
_Descript._] THIS is a small herb, seldom rising above a foot high,
with square hairy, and woody stalks, and two small hoary leaves set at
a joint, about the height of Marjoram, or not much bigger, a little
dented about the edges, and of a very fierce or quick scent, as the
whole herb is: The flowers stand at several spaces of the stalk, from
the middle almost upwards, which are small and gaping like to those of
the Mints, of a pale bluish colour: After which follow small, round
blackish seed. The root is small and woody, with divers small strings
spreading within the ground, and dies not, but abides many years.

_Place._] It grows on heaths, and uplands, and dry grounds, in many
places of this land.

_Time._] They flower in July and their seed is ripe quickly after.

_Government and virtues._] It is an herb of Mercury, and a strong
one too, therefore excellent good in all afflictions of the brain.
The decoction of the herb being drank, brings down women’s courses,
and provokes urine. It is profitable for those that are bursten, or
troubled with convulsions or cramps, with shortness of breath, or
choleric torments and pains in their bellies or stomach; it also helps
the yellow-jaundice, and stays vomiting, being taken in wine. Taken
with salt and honey, it kills all manner of worms in the body. It
helps such as have the leprosy, either taken inwardly, drinking whey
after it, or the green herb outwardly applied. It hinders conception
in women, but either burned or strewed in the chamber, it drives away
venomous serpents. It takes away black and blue marks in the face, and
makes black scars become well coloured, if the green herb (not the
dry) be boiled in wine, and laid to the place, or the place washed
therewith. Being applied to the hucklebone, by continuance of time, it
spends the humours, which cause the pain of the sciatica. The juice
being dropped into the ears, kills the worms in them. The leaves boiled
in wine, and drank, provoke sweat, and open obstructions of the liver
and spleen. It helps them that have a tertian ague (the body being
first purged) by taking away the cold fits. The decoction hereof, with
some sugar put thereto afterwards, is very profitable for those that
be troubled with the over-flowing of the gall, and that have an old
cough, and that are scarce able to breathe by shortness of their wind;
that have any cold distemper in their bowels, and are troubled with
the hardness or the spleen, for all which purposes, both the powder,
called Diacaluminthes, and the compound Syrup of Calamint are the most
effectual. Let no women be too busy with it, for it works very violent
upon the feminine part.

pubmed.title: Extracts of Sideritis scardica and Clinopodium vulgare Alleviate Cognitive Impairments in Scopolamine-Induced Rat Dementia.
pubmed.relevance_note: Supports traditional use for brain afflictions via cognitive impairment models.

pubmed.relevance_note: Reviews broad pharmacological potential including antispasmodic and antioxidant effects.

pubmed.title: Polyphenol Composition, Anticholinesterase and Antioxidant Potential of the Extracts of Clinopodium vulgare L.
pubmed.relevance_note: Demonstrates anticholinesterase activity relevant to cognitive and neuromuscular functions.

evidence.summary: Modern evidence supports Clinopodium vulgare for 'afflictions of the brain' via demonstrated anticholinesterase and cognitive-protective effects in dementia models. Antispasmodic properties may address cramps or convulsions, though specific data for respiratory distress or uterine issues remains limited in current literature.

No relevant modern scientific evidence was found for Pycnanthemum montanum regarding the recorded traditional uses of shortness of breath, uterine issues, or convulsions. While related species in the genus possess antispasmodic properties, specific data for this taxon is currently absent from the retrieved sources.

concordance.rationale: Preclinical evidence (PMID:38339117) supports cognitive impairment claims for Clinopodium vulgare. No clinical data exists for other historical uses like uterine issues or jaundice.
concordance.uncertainty: Taxonomic confusion between Calamint species limits generalization of modern findings to all historical claims.
caveats: No human trials for most claims

issues: Unearned Grade C: The concordance grade 'C' is partially unearned because the rationale cites only preclinical evidence (PMID:38339117) for cognitive impairment, while ignoring that the other historical claims (uterine issues, jaundice) have zero clinical data. A grade of 'C' implies some level of clinical validation or strong consensus which is absent for the majority of the entry's claims.

Missing Evidence for Resolved Taxa: The evidence block lists 0 PubMed entries for Pycnanthemum montanum (Mountain-Mint), yet the entry resolves this taxon with high confidence. There is no supporting literature cited in the evidence block to justify the resolution or any potential claims associated with it.

Incomplete Resolution of Historical Claims: The entry resolves 'Calamint' and 'Mountain-Mint' but fails to provide evidence for the specific historical uses mentioned in the failed quotes (e.g., 'brings down women's courses'). Without evidence, these claims cannot be validated or properly contextualized within the knowledge graph.

Taxonomic Uncertainty Not Mitigated: The reasoning notes taxonomic confusion between Calamint species. However, the entry treats Clinopodium vulgare and Pycnanthemum montanum as distinct resolved entities without clarifying if the historical 'Calamint' name applies to both or just one, leading to potential over-generalization of the preclinical findings from C. vulgare to P. montanum.
